title: Google Confesses AI Search Cuts Revenue, Boosts Ads to Recover Profits
body:
Google’s latest quarterly report laid bare a stark reality for its flagship advertising engine: the rollout of generative‑AI‑driven search has begun to erode the company’s core revenue stream. In the third quarter, the tech giant posted a net cash outflow of $9.06 billion, a dramatic swing that sent its shares sliding sharply on the open. Executives acknowledged that the AI‑enhanced search experience, while hailed as a breakthrough for users, is currently “making less money” than the traditional text‑based model, and they are now doubling down on a surge of new ad formats to stem the bleed.

The earnings release showed that Google’s “Search & Other” segment, which historically accounts for roughly two‑thirds of Alphabet’s total revenue, fell short of analysts’ expectations. Revenue from search ads dropped by 7 percent year‑over‑year, a decline attributed to the company’s own AI experiments that have shifted user behavior toward more conversational, answer‑focused results. Those answers often appear in a single AI‑generated snippet, reducing the number of clickable links and, consequently, the inventory of ad impressions that can be sold alongside them. The impact was felt across the board, from small‑business advertisers who rely on keyword‑driven campaigns to large enterprises that have traditionally invested heavily in Google’s search ecosystem.

In response, Alphabet’s leadership outlined a multi‑pronged strategy aimed at revitalising ad sales within the AI framework. Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler announced the rollout of “AI‑enhanced ad placements” that will embed sponsored content directly into the generative answer boxes, preserving the visual continuity of the AI response while still delivering brand messages. The company also plans to expand its “Performance Max” campaigns, leveraging machine‑learning to automatically allocate budgets across search, display, shopping and video properties, thereby increasing the likelihood that advertisers can capture the limited attention span of AI‑driven users. Early tests of these formats have reportedly yielded click‑through rates up to 30 percent higher than traditional search ads, suggesting a potential path to offset the current shortfall.

Analysts, however, remain cautious. While the introduction of new ad products could plug some of the revenue gap, the fundamental shift in how users interact with information may require deeper structural changes. “Google is essentially trying to re‑monetise a product that it has fundamentally altered,” noted a senior equity analyst at a West Coast investment firm. “If AI answers continue to satisfy user intent in fewer clicks, the overall pool of ad inventory may shrink permanently, forcing the company to look beyond search for growth.” That outlook is reinforced by the broader market trend of advertisers diversifying spend toward social platforms, connected TV, and emerging metaverse environments, all of which promise richer, more immersive brand experiences.

The financial fallout also raises questions about Alphabet’s broader balance sheet health. The $9.06 billion cash outflow, driven largely by accelerated spending on AI research, cloud infrastructure and talent acquisition, has prompted a reassessment of the company’s capital allocation priorities. While the cloud division continues to post robust double‑digit growth, it remains a distant second to the dwindling returns from search. Investors are now watching closely for any signs that the new ad formats can deliver sustainable margins, or whether Alphabet will need to pursue strategic acquisitions or partnerships to bolster its advertising stack.

Looking ahead, Google’s ability to reconcile its AI ambitions with a viable advertising model will be a decisive factor in its financial trajectory. The company has pledged to refine its AI answer boxes to include more contextual ad placements and to roll out advanced measurement tools that give advertisers clearer insight into performance within the AI layer. If these initiatives succeed, they could restore confidence among investors and advertisers alike, stabilising the stock and re‑establishing search as a cash‑generating engine. Conversely, failure to adapt could accelerate a shift away from Google’s once‑dominant ad platform, compelling the tech giant to double‑down on its cloud and hardware ventures as the new pillars of growth. The next quarter will likely reveal whether the AI‑centric ad strategy can bridge the current revenue chasm or if Alphabet must chart a more radical transformation to sustain its market leadership.
